title: Developer Experience: SDK Guides, Quickstarts, API Examples, and Top Support Fixes
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document describes standards and operating procedures for Developer Experience (DevEx) documentation covering SDK guides, quickstarts and templates, API examples, docs-site operating procedures, and the canonical list of top support issues with recommended fixes. It is intended for technical writers, SDK maintainers, developer advocates, and engineers who contribute to public and internal developer docs.

Goals:
- Ensure consistency and high quality across SDK guides and quickstarts so customers onboard quickly and safely.
- Provide canonical API examples (Python, Node, curl) that follow security and performance best practices.
- Capture the top support issues and canonical fixes so support and docs teams can rapidly resolve customer problems.
- Define the docs-site publishing and review workflow to keep content accurate and discoverable.

Audience:
- SDK authors and maintainers
- Developer advocates and solutions engineers
- Support engineers and technical writers
- Product managers and API owners

Contents (high level):
1) SDK guides: required structure and examples
2) Quickstarts & Templates: recommended set and usage patterns
3) API Examples: authentication, streaming, tool-calling patterns
4) Docs-site operating procedures: publishing, review, CI checks
5) Top support issues & canonical fixes

1) SDK GUIDES
Purpose:
Provide a single-source, language-specific reference and onboarding path for customers using Redwood SDKs (Python, JavaScript/Node, Go, Java). SDK guides must be authoritative, include examples, and map back to API reference pages.

Required structure for every SDK guide (use as a template):
- Title and short description (1 sentence)
- Quickstart: 3-5 minute copy-paste example that performs a meaningful action (e.g., create a chat completion + parse a structured response).
- Installation and versioning: supported versions, pip/npm coordinates, and compatibility table.
- Authentication & configuration: environment variables, recommended KMS/hardening notes, example of reading API key from env.
- Common patterns: streaming, retries, timeouts, batching, embeddings usage.
- Error handling: common exceptions, HTTP codes, and retry/backoff guidance.
- Tests & examples: link to a minimal test and to examples repo.
- Release notes & changelog: how to read SDK release notes and migration guides.
- Ownership & support: owner team, Slack channel, and bug-reporting template.

Example Quickstart (Python):
1. pip install redwood-sdk
2. export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-...
3. python
>>> from redwood import RedwoodClient
>>> client = RedwoodClient()
>>> resp = client.chat.create(model="redwood-alpha", messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the following..."}])
>>> print(resp.content)

Release checklist for SDK authors (table):
| Item | Owner | Required before publish |
| Install matrix tested on (py/node versions) | Author | yes |
| Quickstart validated locally | Author | yes |
| Security review (secret handling) | Security | yes |
| API surface documented in reference | API owner | yes |

2) QUICKSTARTS & TEMPLATES
Recommended quickstarts (each must be <10 files, runnable in <2 minutes):
- Chat quickstart (Python + Node) - basic chat, streaming, and structured output
- Embeddings search quickstart - generate embeddings, store to SQLite, search by cosine similarity
- RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) template - simple indexer, retriever, and answer flow
- Cost-optimized batch inference example - shows batching policy + quantized model suggestion
- Private deployment quickstart - how to configure client for Redwood Private (VPC) endpoints

Template repository rules:
- Keep templates minimal and focused on a single use case
- Include a README with objectives, expected outputs, and troubleshooting tips
- Add automated smoke test (CI) that runs the quickstart daily

3) API EXAMPLES
Patterns to include in docs (every example must be copy-paste runnable and secure):
- Authentication patterns: do NOT hardcode API keys in examples. Use environment variables or credential providers.
- Streaming response pattern (Python & Node) with reconnection/resume guidance.
- Function / tool calling examples with typed schemas and input validation.
- Embeddings + vector store example (SQLite or in-memory) with dimensionality notes.
- Retry/backoff pattern for 429s and 5xx errors with recommended backoff policy (exponential, jitter, max 60s).

Canonical curl example (sanitized):
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat\\
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \\
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\
  -d '{"model":"redwood-alpha","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}'

Security notes for API examples:
- Never include real API keys in docs or examples.
- Prefer short-lived tokens or customer-managed proxies in client examples for production guides.

4) DOCS-SITE OPERATING PROCEDURES
Ownership & cadence:
- Docs owner: eng-developer-experience docs team (primary contact: #devex on Slack).
- Review cadence: critical security or API changes - update within 48 hours; non-critical content - review quarterly.

Publishing workflow (high level):
1. Author edits a page in the docs repo (Markdown or AsciiDoc).
2. Create pull request targeting docs-main with summary of changes and affected quickstarts.
3. PR checklist: link to API change, test evidence (smoke test), and reviewer assigned.
4. CI checks: linter, broken link check, code-snippet runnable smoke test.
5. Reviewer approves and docs owner merges.
6. CD pipeline deploys to staging; QA verifies quickstart smoke tests in staging.
7. Deploy to production site and announce on #devex and release notes.

Checklist for reviewers (short):
- Is the quickstart runnable and minimal?
- Are code snippets secure (no keys)?
- Do examples follow current SDK version?
- Are internal links present for troubleshooting and related references?

Docs SLO & incident handling:
- Docs availability target: 99.9% uptime for public docs CDN.
- Content accuracy SLO: critical API docs updated within 48 hours of breaking change.
- If a broken code sample is discovered in production, create an incident in the oncall tracker and roll a hotfix within 24 hours.

5) TOP SUPPORT ISSUES & CANONICAL FIXES (current as of last_updated)
Issue 1: Authentication failures (401) in SDKs\- Symptom: client receives 401 or "invalid_api_key" errors immediately.\- Common root causes: expired key, key copied with surrounding whitespace, wrong environment variable name.\- Canonical fix: verify REDWOOD_API_KEY env var, trim whitespace, show command: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="$(cat ~/.redwood_key | tr -d '\\\\n')". Add guidance for short-lived tokens.

Issue 2: Streaming disconnects mid-response (intermittent)\- Symptom: Partial stream received, then connection reset.\- Root causes: proxy timeouts, client not handling reconnects, using long-polling behind load balancer without keepalive.\- Canonical fix: recommend HTTP/2 or WebSocket streaming endpoints, add client-side resume logic, set ALB idle timeout > 120s for streaming endpoints.

Issue 3: High latency for small payloads when batching is enabled\- Symptom: single-request latency spikes to 1000+ ms.\- Root causes: aggressive batching configuration in client or gateway.\- Canonical fix: provide recommended per-route batching config (max_batch_size=8, max_batch_latency_ms=25) and show how to override per-route.

Issue 4: Incorrect structured output parsing\- Symptom: Model returns unexpected keys or formats.\- Root causes: missing schema enforcement or non-deterministic instructions.\- Canonical fix: use function/tool calling with strict JSON schema; include example schema and validation step in quickstart.

Issue 5: Embedding dimension mismatch errors\- Symptom: "dimension mismatch" when inserting into vector store.\- Root causes: different model used to generate embeddings for index vs query.\- Canonical fix: always record model id and embedding dimensionality in metadata; add runtime check in ingestion pipeline.

Issue 6: Private deployment endpoint connectivity (TLS)\- Symptom: TLS handshake failures or certificate errors when connecting to Private control plane.\- Root causes: missing CA certs, client not trusting customer-managed CA, incorrect endpoint.\- Canonical fix: verify CA bundle on client host, provide command to install CA into system store, and include fallback to use redwoodctl to validate endpoint: redwoodctl healthcheck --endpoint https://private.example.com

Escalation matrix and when to involve other teams:
- If issue is reproducible and affects > 1 customer for a specific SDK, tag @eng-serving-runtime and @eng-sre and open a P1 if production customer-facing.
- For security-sensitive issues (keys leaked, token misuse), immediately notify Security and follow incident response playbook.
